title: Ringtones, an Overdrawn Card and Cellulant's Turn to Banking
dek: Cellulant began in Nairobi selling ringtones; when the operators kept most of the money, its founders built banking tools nobody bought, until M-Pesa changed the market.

story.event: Abandoning the ringtone business and building mobile banking tools through lean years until banks came asking after M-Pesa
story.summary: Cellulant, set up in 2004 by Ken Njoroge and Bolaji Akinboro, began by selling ringtones through mobile operators, which kept about 80 per cent of the money. Njoroge abandoned the model and built bank-payment and mobile-banking software that at first found no buyers, while Akinboro's salary and overdrawn debit card kept the company alive. After Safaricom launched M-Pesa in 2007, banks asked Cellulant to build their mobile banking, and it grew into a pan-African payments company.
paragraphs: In 2004 Ken Njoroge, a Kenyan software developer who had already co-founded a small web company, met Bolaji Akinboro, a Nigerian pharmacist then working with the World Bank on the African Virtual University. Mobile phones were spreading fast across Africa, and Njoroge believed, he said later, that "all services we see on the internet will move into the mobile environment." After pitching to Uganda Telecom, they registered Cellulant in Britain, reckoning that incorporating in Uganda, Kenya or Nigeria would take at least three months.

By the first board meeting, that same year, the finances were, Njoroge recalled, "not in the best of conditions." The first business was music. Cellulant sold ringtones through the mobile networks and paid musicians a share of what fans spent on their songs. The trouble was the split: the operators kept about 80 per cent, Business Daily later reported. A Cellulant executive has also described how hard it was to bill customers through prepaid airtime in those years. Njoroge gave up on the model.

Lean years followed. Using his IT skills, Njoroge built a system that let people spend their bank savings on goods and withdraw cash; no buyer came forward. He then built a platform for account holders to run their bank accounts from a computer or an internet-ready phone. Akinboro paid for it all from his World Bank job, repeatedly overstretching his debit card, while Njoroge had no income and, Business Daily reported, worried constantly. Cellulant came close to shutting. Approaching banks to bill music fans from their accounts had, the executive said, revealed a larger problem: banks had few ways to serve ordinary retail customers.

The opening came with M-Pesa, the mobile money service Safaricom launched in March 2007. With its success, Njoroge said in 2010, banks were finally waking up to mobile banking, and Cellulant had already built the plumbing. Offers came to build online and mobile banking for several banks, and when they wanted the same in their Ugandan and Tanzanian subsidiaries, Cellulant followed. Its first banking product simply let customers check their balances. A 2010 profile reported that it had turned profitable in 2007 and grown from two people to more than 90. By 2016 it served 50 banks through 40 mobile operators.

quote.text: Unvexed if his work fail, if it succeed Unflattered, in his own heart justified, Quit of debates and doubts, his is "true" act
quote.locator: Chapter XVIII (verse 10 in the usual numbering)
quote.source_title: The Song Celestial; Or, Bhagavad-Gîtâ, tr. Sir Edwin Arnold, Project Gutenberg eBook #2388
quote.connection: The Gita describes right action as work done unvexed when it fails and unflattered when it succeeds. Njoroge and Akinboro were plainly vexed: one worried constantly, the other overdrew his card. What they share with the ideal is narrower, and harder: they kept doing the work before anything rewarded it.

reflection: Look at the order of events. The ringtones sold, but most of the money went elsewhere. The next two products found no buyers. The thing that finally worked was built in the lean years, before anyone wanted it, and what changed was the market, not the founders' cleverness.

You do not have to feel serene to keep going, whatever the Gita hopes for. It may be enough to be honest about who is carrying the cost while you do. In this story it was Akinboro's salary and his overdrawn card. In yours it might be a partner, a parent or a colleague covering for you, and they deserve to hear that you have noticed.
invitation: Think of one person who is quietly carrying part of the cost of your work, at home or at work. Tell them today, in one plain sentence, that you see it.

cross_checks.claim: Cellulant began by selling ringtones and other music content through mobile operators.
Cellulant moved from music content into mobile banking for banks.
Njoroge and Akinboro started the company in 2004, with Akinboro then working with the World Bank on the African Virtual University.
M-Pesa's success turned banks towards mobile banking, which brought Cellulant its banking business.
Akinboro's World Bank job funded the company in its early years.

research_notes: Dates: no source dates each step of the change. The founding year is 2004 in Njoroge's own words (How we made it in Africa, 2010 and 2018) and in Business Daily (2016, 2023); other profiles give 2002 or 2003, and The Standard's '18 years' as chief executive by 2021 implies 2003; the story uses 2004. The story dates only the M-Pesa launch (March 2007) and the reported profitability (2007), and presents the abandoned ringtone model and the unsold products as preceding the bank offers, which is the order Business Daily (2016) gives; approx_date is 2007, not the slate's 2006. Why the ringtone business stalled: Business Daily (2016) says operators kept about 80 per cent; Business Daily (2023), quoting chief revenue officer David Waithaka, stresses the difficulty of billing through airtime; The Standard (2021) says the model became unsustainable once advanced phones let users store their own music, which describes a later period. The story gives the first two, attributed, and omits the third. Cellulant also kept a content business alongside banking (How we made it in Africa, 2010, lists mobile content, mobile money and mobile business services), so the story describes Njoroge giving up the ringtone model rather than the company leaving content entirely. Outcome numbers: How we made it in Africa (2010) says Cellulant sold more than 16,000 ringtones at KSh 75 each on its first day in Kenya, yet made about KSh 60,000 a month in its first year; these do not sit together (and a newsletter gives a different price), so the story uses neither. The same 2010 profile gives both 'over six million subscribers' and 'over 12 million customers'; neither is used. Bank counts vary over time (50 banks in 2016, more than 60 in 2023, about 100 by 2021 per The Standard); the story uses the 2016 figure with its date. Funding: Business Daily (2016) says Akinboro's World Bank pay financed the venture and that the founders later gave up 50 per cent and then a further 16 per cent to investors to fund growth; that later equity came after the episode, so 'bootstrapped' describes this period. Nairametrics describes Akinboro's role as strategic and financial support from a board position. The Waithaka quotations are paraphrased and attributed to 'a Cellulant executive'. TechCabal, cellulant.io and carolmusyoka.com block automated requests and are not cited. Wikipedia is used once, only for the M-Pesa launch date.
